2caec2529b:
Iteration and errors look like separate subjects. They are not. A for loop ends because an exception, StopIteration, is raised and caught for you. A file closes because a context manager's __exit__ runs even when the body blows up.

This chapter covers the machinery that makes Python programs robust. First comes how iteration really works, how to stream data lazily with generators, and how with guarantees cleanup. Then comes the everyday toolkit: exceptions, modules, files, logging, debugging, configuration, and packaging your work so it runs the same way twice.
ed63a5aa77:
Three terms matter here.

  • An iterable is any object you can loop over. Technically, it defines __iter__(), which returns an iterator.
  • An iterator is the object that does the actual stepping. It defines __next__(), which returns the next item or raises StopIteration when the items run out. Its __iter__() returns itself, so an iterator can go anywhere an iterable is expected.
  • A protocol is an informal interface: no base class required, just the right methods with the right behavior.

Python leans on protocols everywhere. Iteration is the first one worth memorizing.
489732d8a8: That is the whole trick. for calls iter() on the object. Then it calls next() repeatedly until StopIteration, which it swallows silently. The exception is not an error here. It is the agreed signal for "done," and for is the code that agreed to listen for it.
2e8cb48ff2:
The class makes one distinction visible: Countdown is an iterator, not merely an iterable. A list is iterable but not an iterator. next([1, 2]) raises TypeError, because the list has no __next__. You must call iter() on it first.

Iterators are single-pass. Once a Countdown hits zero, it stays finished. Looping over it again yields nothing, because __iter__ returns the same spent object. Containers like lists avoid this. Each iter() call builds a brand-new iterator, so you can loop as many times as you like.
ba7979bbf0: A realistic use is paginated APIs. Each response gives you a page and a hint whether more pages exist. An iterator models that shape exactly: one __next__ per page, and StopIteration when the pages run out.
47607aa412:
A few edge cases are worth knowing.

  • An infinite iterator, one whose __next__ never raises, is legal. for will never terminate on it. Only use one with a manual break or a tool like itertools.islice (see 6.2).
  • Inside a generator, letting StopIteration escape the frame is an error. Since Python 3.7 it becomes RuntimeError, per PEP 479. Raise it only from __next__, never from inside generator bodies.
  • If you write __iter__ on a container, return a fresh iterator each call. Otherwise your container will mysteriously work exactly once.
c2f562b88c: Write a custom iterator when the stepping logic carries state: pagination cursors, countdowns, merging sorted streams. For most one-off sequences, a generator function (next section) is shorter and harder to get wrong. The class form earns its keep in two cases. One is when the iterator needs methods beyond __next__. The other is when several loops must share the same in-progress state.
b28af22cf8: Practice task A1. Write an iterator class EvenNumbers(limit). It yields even numbers starting from 0, up to and including limit. list(EvenNumbers(10)) should give [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]. Then show it is single-pass: loop over the same object twice and observe the second loop yields nothing. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
aec5df6a7c: Building a list of a million items just to loop over it once wastes memory. It also makes you wait for the whole computation before the first item is usable. Some sequences never end at all. Generators solve this. A generator computes each item on demand and pauses between items, holding almost no memory.
599ddf04f1:
A generator function is any function containing yield. Calling it does not run the body. It returns a generator object, which is an iterator.

The body runs only when something calls next(). Each yield pauses the function and hands a value out. The next next() resumes right after that yield. This start-stop behavior is laziness: work happens only when a value is actually pulled.
1e7f418114: Generators are single-pass, and that bites everyone exactly once. A consumed generator stays consumed. Looping over it again silently yields nothing. There's no error, just an empty result that can look like a data bug.
96b103efdf:
When the same generator feeds two consumers, the fix is structural. Either make a small factory function that returns a fresh generator, or materialize a list once.

Debugging tip: if a pipeline mysteriously produces empty output on its second run, check whether a generator got consumed by the first.
6fbd1a3b92: Here is the realistic shape. Small generator stages are chained together, each pulling from the previous one. The final stage writes through a context-managed file (context managers get their own section next). Nothing is stored except the item currently moving through the pipe.
a8f365a78c:
More edge cases:

  • Generators have no length and no indexing. len(gen) raises TypeError. If you need either, you did not want a generator.
  • A return value inside a generator does not produce an item. The value lands on the StopIteration that ends iteration. Almost nobody reads it, so do not rely on it.
  • yield inside try/finally works. The finally runs when the generator is closed or garbage-collected, which is useful for releasing resources held across yields.
  • breaking out of a loop over a generator abandons it. That is fine; the generator is simply discarded.
63cb3d30d1: Reach for generators for pipelines, large files, paginated streams, and anything infinite. Skip them when you need to iterate twice, check the length, or index into results. Skip them too when you share the data with code that expects a sequence. In those cases build the list. Laziness is a tool, not a virtue.
9b90dbe459: Practice task A2. Write a generator function running_total(numbers). It takes any iterable of numbers and yields the running total after each item: list(running_total([12.5, 7.0, 20.0])) gives [12.5, 19.5, 39.5]. Then feed it a generator expression and confirm it works on lazy input too. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
f8473afad3:
Every program has setup/teardown pairs. You open a file and close it. You acquire a lock and release it. You start a database transaction and commit or roll it back.

The naive pattern is setup, then work, then teardown. It breaks the moment the work raises. The teardown never runs, and the resource leaks. try/finally fixes it but litters every call site with boilerplate. Context managers put the pairing in one reusable place, and the with statement guarantees the teardown runs.
1109bea261:
A context manager is any object with __enter__ and __exit__ methods. The with statement calls __enter__ first and runs the body. Then it calls __exit__, on normal completion and on exception alike.

__exit__ receives three arguments describing the exception, or three Nones when the body finished cleanly. Its return value matters. A truthy return suppresses the exception, and execution continues after the with block as if nothing happened. A falsy return (or None) lets the exception propagate after cleanup.
599dd80d10: Now watch the exception path. The body raises, and __exit__ still runs its cleanup. Because it returns False, the exception continues outward to whoever catches it.
0c5304c781: Suppression is the sharp edge. Returning True from __exit__ swallows the exception. Occasionally that is exactly right, such as skipping a record you know is harmless. Usually it's a way to hide bugs. Suppress narrowly, and say so out loud in the code.
382926986f:
The standard library ships context managers you will use constantly.

  • open() is one. Files close themselves at the end of the with block, exception or not. That's why every file example in this chapter uses it.
  • contextlib.suppress is the ready-made version of the class above.
  • contextlib.redirect_stdout captures prints, handy in tests.
  • contextlib.contextmanager is for writing your own. It turns a generator function into a context manager. Code before the yield is __enter__, and code after (in finally) is __exit__.

The decorator is the simpler alternative to the class form for straightforward setup/teardown.
df2c740d78:
A few more things come up in real code.

  • You can open several managers in one statement: with open(a) as fa, open(b) as fb:.
  • When the number of managers is not known up front, contextlib.ExitStack handles a dynamic set.
  • If __exit__ itself raises, the new exception replaces the one being handled. So keep __exit__ simple and total.
  • The value after as is whatever __enter__ returned. That's why open() gives you the file object.
7396f612c1: Use a context manager for every acquire/release pair: files, locks (threading.Lock supports with), database transactions, temporary directory changes. Do not use one for plain computation with no resource involved. A function call is clearer. Prefer @contextmanager for simple cases. Use the class form when the manager needs real state or methods.
8e22d0b6ab: Practice task A3. Write a class-based context manager Stopwatch(label). In __enter__, it records the start time using time.perf_counter(). In __exit__, it prints f"{label}: {elapsed:.4f}s" and stores the elapsed time on self.elapsed. It must never suppress exceptions. Verify with a with Stopwatch("summing"): block around sum(range(1_000_000)). The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
ee46ec9a3a: An exception is Python's way of saying "I cannot continue this operation." Something goes wrong, and Python builds an exception object describing it. That object travels up the call stack until something catches it or the program exits. The traceback is the travel log. Learn to read it and half of debugging is done.
ca71dd5067:
Read it from the bottom. ZeroDivisionError: division by zero is the what. Then climb. It happened in load_price at the division. That was called from a generator expression inside total, which was called from the module top level. The data came from cart, and the second item has "quantity": 0.

The fix is in the data, or in validation before the division. The traceback told you where, and the code tells you why.
4b55fbb665:
You raise exceptions with raise, and catch them with try/except. The full try statement has four parts, each with a job:

  • try holds the risky code.
  • except handles specific failures.
  • else runs only when nothing failed. It keeps the try block small, so you catch only what you meant to.
  • finally runs no matter what: success, exception, even return. Use it for cleanup that is not already owned by a context manager.
01b9198300: Custom exceptions should subclass Exception, not BaseException. The reason is concrete. BaseException is also the parent of SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt. Code that catches Exception, which is most error handling, will not catch those. So Ctrl+C and sys.exit() keep working. Subclassing BaseException directly opts your error out of every normal except Exception handler. That is almost never what you want.
5ec892edd2:
Exception chaining answers "what caused what." When you raise a new exception inside an except block, Python links them.

Do it explicitly with raise ... from .... The original becomes __cause__, and the traceback prints "The above exception was the direct cause." Without from, the original is still attached as __context__ ("During handling of the above exception..."), but __cause__ stays None. Explicit is better, because it says you translated the error on purpose.
363e8cad6f: Chain when you translate a low-level error into a domain error: ValueError into ConfigError, or an OSError into your own StorageError. The caller sees your meaningful message. The original is one attribute away when they need the details. Use raise ... from None to deliberately hide the original. Do that only when the original would confuse more than it helps.
bbbc3b352a: Watch for two mistakes. First, catching an exception and raising a new one without from still chains implicitly. The traceback stays informative. That is fine; just know it happens. Second, never raise inside finally casually. It replaces whatever exception was in flight and destroys the original traceback.
651917957f: Catching is easy. Catching well is a discipline with one rule: catch at the boundary where you can act. Deep inside a parser, you usually cannot do anything useful about a failure, so let it propagate. At the boundary, you can retry, fall back to a default, or tell the user something intelligible. The boundary is the request handler, the config loader, the main loop. That is where try/except belongs.
955c4c7cd5: The classic bug is the bare except:. It catches everything, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. The version below does not even log. Real bugs vanish into it, and you learn about them from users, weeks later.
22fa4e1bda: A note on that output order: the WARNING line appears first even though the buggy call ran first. Logging writes to stderr and print writes to stdout. The two streams interleave when merged. Inside a terminal they usually appear in order; when piped or captured, expect surprises. It is not a bug in your program.
19d1368ca1:
except Exception is better than bare except, because it spares KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. But it is still too broad for most code. It swallows TypeErrors from your own typos alongside the ValueError you expected. Name the exception you expect.

Sometimes you genuinely need a wide net, such as a top-level crash handler or a worker loop that must not die. Then log the full traceback with logging.exception(...) inside the except block, and re-raise or exit deliberately. A caught-and-logged error is handled. A caught-and-silenced error is a future outage.
6e7692f933: Two more habits. First, keep try blocks small. Wrap only the line that can fail, so the except cannot accidentally catch an error from unrelated code. Second, when in doubt, re-raise with a bare raise. It re-raises the current exception with its traceback intact. That's how a boundary logs and then lets the caller decide.
b11074b340:
Practice task B1/B2. Write a small config loader.

  • parse_line(line) splits a "key=value" line and converts the value with int(). On failure it raises a custom ConfigError chained from the original with raise ... from ....
  • load_config(lines) skips blank lines and # comments and calls parse_line inside a try. On ConfigError it logs a warning (including the chained cause) and keeps going with defaults.

Show it handling ["retries=5", "timeout=oops", "# comment", "workers=4"]. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
e68d45342a:
One file works until it doesn't. At a few hundred lines, splitting code into modules stops being organization and starts being survival.

A module is a Python file. Importing it runs its top-level code once and binds its names. A package is a directory of modules, marked by an __init__.py file. That makes it a regular package; directories without one can also work as namespace packages.

Imports come in two flavors. Absolute imports name the full path from the project root (from shop.cart import Cart). Relative imports use dots for the current package (from .cart import Cart) and only work inside packages.
f017642484: Every module has a __name__. Imported, it is the module's dotted path. Run directly as a script, it is "__main__". The if __name__ == "__main__": guard uses that to separate "library behavior" from "script behavior." The same file can be imported quietly and also run standalone for demos or CLIs.
68b017c27c:
Two import mistakes account for most beginner suffering.

First, running a file inside a package directly as a script (python pkg/mod.py) breaks relative imports. The file no longer knows its package. Run it as python -m pkg.mod from the project root instead. The -m flag preserves the package context.

Second, naming your file after a standard module (json.py, random.py) shadows the real one and produces bewildering errors. Python 3.13 even hints at this in some import errors.
4507f7a074: The nastiest import failure is the circular import: module A imports B, and B imports A. Python handles this badly only when a name is needed at import time. Watch what happens. Here is the real ImportError from Python 3.13.16 (path shortened):
8f850a2640:
Here are the mechanics. Importing circ_a starts executing it, which imports circ_b. That module tries from circ_a import VALUE_A. But circ_a is only half-executed, and VALUE_A does not exist yet.

The fix is structural, not syntactic. Move the shared names into a third module that both import (circ_common.py here), so the dependency arrows point one way. Stubborn cases have two alternatives. You can import inside the function that needs the name, deferring the import until call time. Or you can merge the two modules if they were never really separate.
b59cced2b9:
Prefer absolute imports everywhere. They read unambiguously and survive files moving between packages. Use relative imports only for intra-package references where the package might be renamed.

And keep import cycles out by design. Shared constants and helpers go in a low-level module, and high-level modules import downward. If two modules genuinely need each other, that is the design telling you they are one module.
b97e2a81c7: String paths are a trap. "data" + "/" + name breaks on Windows, and ~ never expands. Typos surface as missing files three directories away from the bug. pathlib.Path replaces string hacking with an object that joins with /, knows its parts, and works across operating systems.
fe2d352e2b:
Use Path for everything:

  • p.exists() and p.is_file()
  • p.glob("*.csv"), and p.rglob("*") for recursive search
  • p.read_text() / p.write_text() for small files

For large files, open() in a with block streams without loading everything into memory. Reach for os.path only when maintaining old code. pathlib is the modern spelling and the one to learn.
efa3501a1d: JSON has two gotchas. First, it has no date or set type. json.dumps({1, 2}) and json.dumps(datetime.now()) raise TypeError, so convert those yourself. Second, true/false/null in the file become True/False/None on load. The round trip is faithful for the types JSON supports.
18e0ad2f56: CSV is the interchange format for flat rows. The csv module handles quoting and embedded commas that naive split(",") mangles. Two rules apply. Always open the file with newline="": the csv module owns line endings, and without it you get blank rows on Windows. And remember the reader gives you strings, so convert columns yourself.
20f660e426:
A version note, because this bites people. In Python 3.13, open() without an encoding argument still follows your locale. It is not guaranteed UTF-8. Pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly, as every example in this chapter does. (PEP 686 makes UTF-8 the default encoding, but that lands in Python 3.15. See https://peps.python.org/pep-0686/ and the 3.13 docs for open().)

The errors= parameter controls decode failures. "strict" (the default) raises, "replace" substitutes �, and "ignore" drops the bytes. For reading untrusted files, "replace" keeps the program alive. For files you wrote, "strict" surfaces corruption instead of hiding it.
87ccd1937d: Resource cleanup ties back to 6.3. Open files in with blocks so they close on every path, including exceptions. An unclosed file usually gets collected eventually. But "usually" is how you lose the last buffered write.
d2366c6ed0: Practice task B4. Write a CSV-to-JSON converter. Read /tmp/ch06_inventory.csv (columns sku,qty,price). Convert qty to int and price to float. Write the list of dicts to /tmp/ch06_inventory.json with indent=2. Use newline="", encoding="utf-8", and with blocks throughout. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
fb2f751e00:
print debugging works until the program grows past one terminal. The grown-up toolkit has four parts:

  • logging for observability
  • the debugger for inspection
  • assertions for invariants
  • environment-driven configuration
de0ceb4e12:
Logging records what happened, at a severity. The levels, lowest to highest, are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. Set the threshold with basicConfig. Get a named logger per module with getLogger(__name__), and log at the level that matches.

basicConfig configures the root logger. Call it once, in your program's entry point, never inside a library module.
5d0ee82e22: For production you will want timestamps, file handlers, and structured formats. The logging module supports all of it, and the stdlib docs cover the recipes. The habit to build now: log at the right level, include the values you will need later, and never print in library code.
2be2ea5d8c: Debugging starts with the traceback (6.4). Sometimes the traceback is not enough. The traceback module lets you capture one for a handled error and keep going: log it, skip the bad record, continue the loop.
fd9df83115:
When you need to inspect live state, breakpoint() drops you into pdb, the built-in debugger, at that line. (Set the PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 environment variable and every breakpoint() becomes a no-op. That's useful when a stray one reaches production.)

The essential commands are p <expr> to print a value, n to run the next line, c to continue, and q to quit. Here is a real pdb session, driven by piped input (paths shortened):
2275433491:
Each p total shows the running sum (1, 3, 6), and c resumes until the next breakpoint. pdb has far more commands: l to list source, s to step into calls, w for the stack. But p, n, c, q cover most sessions.

One caution: never commit a breakpoint() to a shared branch. It halts whoever runs the code.
1b839d7c68:
Assertions guard programmer errors, things that must be true if your code is correct. assert condition, message raises AssertionError when the condition fails.

The critical fact: python -O strips all asserts. So asserts are for invariants, never for validating user input or external data. If the check must run in production, raise a real exception.
50d3693891: The second call computed -50.0, and nothing printed it. With -O the asserts vanish. No AssertionError is raised, and the except block never runs. The bug sailed through invisible. That is the whole lesson: asserts are development scaffolding, not validation.
3d4f6a275a: Configuration keeps environment-specific values out of your code. The simplest pattern that scales is to read environment variables with os.environ.get. Always give a default, and convert types yourself, since env vars are strings.
6a4853405b:
For a real project, put get_config() in a small config.py module and import it where needed. That gives you one place that knows every setting and its default. Never commit secrets to the repo. They arrive as environment variables from the deploy environment.

(Third-party helpers like python-dotenv load a local .env file into os.environ for development. That is library behavior, not stdlib. It's fine to use; just know which side of the line it sits on.)
a267ed6ac9: Practice task B5. Add observability to a function. Write shipping_cost(weight_kg). It asserts the weight is non-negative and reads a base fee from the SHIP_BASE env var (default "5.0"). It computes base + 1.25 * weight_kg, logs the inputs and result at INFO, and returns the cost. Demonstrate the default and an overridden env value. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.
aca2a3e930:
Your project needs requests==2.32.3. Another project needs requests==2.28.1. Installing both globally is impossible. This is dependency hell, and virtual environments are the exit.

A venv is a directory with its own Python and its own site-packages. Each project gets one, and their dependencies never meet.
5ed77abc40: Inside the venv, pip installs into the venv, not the system. A requirements.txt file pins what the project needs, one name==version per line. Then pip install -r requirements.txt reproduces the environment anywhere:
cce0ef2f59:
Two conventions keep projects sane. The first is layout.

  • A flat layout (myapp.py plus tests/) is fine for small tools.
  • A src layout (src/mypkg/, tests/ at the root) prevents a classic accident: importing the local package instead of the installed one. It is also what packaging tools expect once you publish.

Either way, tests live in a top-level tests/ directory, next to the code, never inside the package.
4dbd21c2bd: The second is a reproducible run command. python -m demoapp runs the demoapp package's __main__.py with the project root on sys.path. It's the same invocation on your machine, your teammate's, and CI. It beats python demoapp/__main__.py, which breaks package-relative imports (the 6.6 mistake). Here is a minimal package and the run, executed for real:
9548170fac: And here is the same run inside the fresh venv from above. It proves the environment is truly isolated:
d8b685d2fc: The habit, stated once: one venv per project, dependencies pinned in requirements.txt, tests in tests/, and python -m as the run command. Do that from the first commit, and "works on my machine" stops being a sentence you say.
1cf30a8832: Try looping over one object twice: ev = EvenNumbers(10); list(ev); list(ev). The second list() is []. Single-pass, as promised.
